description: Render-time sanitisation floor — SEMANTIC-invariant fixtures, not byte-parity ones. Each case is a slot payload plus the invariant a conformant rendering host must satisfy; the rendered markup around it differs legitimately per host, so nothing here is compared byte-for-byte. This manifest is HAND-AUTHORED and is not emitted by any host's corpus generator (unlike the root manifest.json, which is generated and would overwrite hand-added entries).

invariants.reject: The floor MUST refuse the payload. A host either omits the attribute or substitutes the literal `about:blank` (WIRE_FORMAT.md §19 rule 6).
invariants.accept: The floor MUST accept the payload and emit `expected` — the §19 rule 1 normalised form, which is not always the input.
invariants.inert: The payload must not survive into the rendered output as LIVE MARKUP. It may appear as TEXT. Checked as `forbiddenPattern` — case-insensitive regexes that must not match the host's rendered output — because the markup around the payload differs legitimately per host and byte comparison is therefore unavailable. A case may also carry `required`: substrings that MUST appear, which is how a legitimate case pins that escaping was not 'fixed' into stripping.

reasons.off-origin: The WHATWG URL parser resolves this to a DIFFERENT origin than the containing document. On a link that is navigation the tree never asked for; on an image source it is an off-origin request that leaks the referrer.
reasons.same-origin: The parser resolves this within the containing document's origin, so refusing it would be a false positive.
reasons.scheme-refused: Rules 2-4 classify the scheme and default-deny it.

deliberateOverRejection: A case carrying `"overRejects": true` is one where the floor refuses a payload the URL parser would have resolved harmlessly. That is intentional — rule 2 strips everything at or below U+0020 from the scheme candidate, which is stricter than the parser's TAB/LF/CR removal, and over-rejection is the safe direction. The flag exists so a checker that resolves each `input` against a conformant parser (the only honest way to verify the `off-origin` and `same-origin` claims here) can tell a deliberate divergence from a wrong fixture, instead of every future reader re-deriving the distinction.

groups.description: The URL-scheme floor, and specifically §19 rule 1 — that the floor normalises the string exactly as the URL Standard's basic URL parser does before inspecting it. Every `off-origin` case below was verified against a WHATWG-conformant parser by resolving it against the base `https://good.example/page` and comparing origins; the `same-origin` cases the same way.

cases.note: The base case rule 5 has always caught.
The parser folds `\` to `/` for special schemes, so all four two-separator spellings resolve identically.
V1. Without rule 1 step 2 the first two characters are `/` and TAB, so a positional test reads an ordinary relative reference; the parser removes the tab and resolves off-origin.
V1 crossed with the backslash spellings — the two evasions compose.
V1 with LF. Step 2 removes TAB, LF and CR — all three, from anywhere.
V1 with CR.
An interleaved run — the same defect wearing more characters. A host that removed only the FIRST occurrence would pass every single-character case above and fail here.
V2. No language's native trim removes U+0001, so the two slashes sat at positions 1 and 2 and a positional test never saw them; step 1 removes the whole C0-or-space range.
V2 with NUL — the same class.
V2 at the top of the C0 range. U+001C-U+001F is where the hosts measurably disagreed before rule 1 went ASCII-exact: Python's native strip removed them, the other four did not.
Step 1 trims BOTH ends, and the whole C0-or-space range at each.
Rule 1's output is what gets EMITTED, not the input. This is the case that makes adopting rule 1 a breaking change for a host: accepted bytes move.

Step 2 is TAB/LF/CR ONLY. The parser removes U+000B at the edges and KEEPS it in the interior, so this is an ordinary same-origin path. A host that widened step 2 to 'all C0' would over-reject here — which is why this case is an accept, not an omission.
As above, for U+000C.

Rule 1 is ASCII-exact, so non-ASCII whitespace survives — and the parser keeps it too, resolving a same-origin path. A native trim removed it, the floor then saw `//`, and rejected: a false positive this case pins as gone.

U+0085 NEL is where JS diverged from the other four hosts before rule 1 went ASCII-exact: `String.prototype.trim` keeps it; .NET, Python, Go and Rust all removed it. Same false positive, different four hosts.
A SINGLE leading backslash is not protocol-relative — the parser reads it as `/evil.example`, an ordinary same-origin path. Pinned so the guard is never widened into a same-origin regression.
Rule 2 is unchanged by rule 1 and still classifies this as `javascript`. This case is why V1 and V2 are off-origin navigation rather than script execution.

Rule 2's below-U+0020 strip is deliberately STRICTER than the parser, which removes only TAB/LF/CR and so reads this as a relative path resolving SAME-ORIGIN. Over-rejection is the safe direction; do not narrow rule 2 to rule 1's TAB/LF/CR set to 'make them consistent'. This is the corpus's only case where the floor and the parser deliberately disagree.
An empty result is accepted and passed through — a same-page reference, the documented HTML behaviour.
Normalises to empty, and therefore takes the empty branch rather than reaching rule 2.

groups.description: Hostile payloads in a markdown-bearing slot. The payload classes are seeded from the reference host's own adversarial corpus, and the split-tag cases are the ones worth understanding: removing an inner tag REASSEMBLES a live one from the fragments either side, so a single-pass stripper passes every other case here and fails those two.
groups.appliesTo: Hosts that render markdown to markup. A host with no markup sink declares this group not-applicable.

cases.note: The base case. Escaping by construction or stripping both satisfy the invariant.
A stripper that removes one balanced block and stops leaves the inner one live.
The classic single-pass evasion: removing the inner tag REASSEMBLES a live one from the fragments either side. A stripper that does not re-scan passes every other case here and fails this one.
The same evasion on the closing tag.
Case folding must be ASCII-only and must not desynchronise offsets (§19's case-folding rule).
Whitespace inside the tag: a matcher anchored on the exact string `<script>` misses it.
A tab where a space is expected. HTML treats both as attribute separators.
A newline inside the tag — the same class as the tab, and the one a line-oriented scan misses.
No closing tag. A stripper requiring a balanced pair must still neutralise this.
A framing vector rather than a scripting one; the same obligation.
As above, via a plugin element.
An inline handler on an otherwise ordinary anchor. The pattern matches a live tag interior, not the attribute name — an escaped payload legitimately still contains the text `onclick=`.
The most-used handler vector, because a broken image fires it with no user interaction.
The handler separated from the tag name by a newline rather than a space.
Case-varied handler name.
A dangerous scheme reaching an href through the markdown path rather than a URL slot.

nonGoals.why: A `/`-separated attribute is valid HTML5 but a shape the deterministic markdown renderer never emits, so the defence-in-depth sweep deliberately does not chase it. Recorded, not asserted.

The sweep does not HTML-entity-decode before matching. The renderer escapes by construction and never emits an attacker-controlled entity-encoded scheme, so this stays a stated gap rather than a silent one.

The raw-HTML substring sweep does not normalise intra-scheme whitespace. The render path never reaches it with such a URL, because the URL floor (§19 rule 2) normalises and refuses it upstream — which the `url-floor` group asserts directly.

groups.description: Hostile payloads in a plain text-bearing slot. There is no markup language in play, so the whole payload is content and must arrive as content — including the legitimate case, which is pinned so that escaping is never 'fixed' into stripping.
groups.appliesTo: Hosts that render text into markup. A host with no markup sink declares this group not-applicable.

cases.note: A text slot is not a markup slot. The payload is content, and must arrive as content.
The handler vector through a text slot. Forbidding the live tag is the whole check: with no tag open, the handler inside it cannot be an attribute.

The legitimate case, and the only one carrying `required`. Ordinary prose must survive ESCAPED rather than stripped — pinned because 'nothing forbidden appeared' is equally true of output that threw the content away.
A payload that tries to close the element it is inside before opening its own.

groups.description: The consumer-side attribute hatch. The KEY gate is a positive character allowlist rather than a prefix rule alone, because HTML has no escape for an illegal character in an attribute name: a key that terminates its own name is not a mangled attribute, it is several attributes, one of which can be a live handler. The VALUE gate is deliberately weaker — both renderers escape values, so it is defence in depth under that escaping, not a replacement for it.
groups.appliesTo: Hosts that emit consumer-supplied attributes. A host that does not expose the hatch declares this group not-applicable.

cases.note: Any `on*` handler, however constructed.
The reject is case-insensitive.
A CSS-injection vector, out of scope by design rather than omission.
Outside the `data-*` / `aria-*` allowlist.

The canonical attribute-NAME injection: prefix-valid, but the space and `=` open a second, live attribute at any emission site that writes names raw. HTML has no escape for an illegal character in a name, so rejection is the only sound response.
The same class, shorter.
`=` starts a value.
A quote can terminate the attribute in a quoted context.
Angle brackets can terminate the tag.
A `/` separates attributes in HTML5.
A tab separates attributes.
A newline separates attributes.
A NUL byte, which some parsers treat as a terminator.
The legitimate case. Pinned so tightening the gate cannot silently break the test-hook convention it exists to permit.
As above, for accessibility attributes.
Hyphens inside the suffix are legal.
Angle brackets in a value. Rejected as defence in depth UNDER the renderers' value escaping, never as a replacement for it.
A control byte in a value.
Quotes are deliberately NOT rejected in a value: both renderers escape values, which is what makes a quote inert. Pinned so the gate is not tightened into breaking ordinary text.
The ordinary case.
Tab is the one C0 character permitted in a value — pinned because the rule is easy to 'tidy' into rejecting all control characters.

invariantInertNote: A PATTERN rather than a plain substring, and the distinction is load-bearing rather than fussy. An escaped payload still CONTAINS the string `onclick=` — as text, harmlessly — so a substring check for it fails a CORRECT host. The obligation is that no LIVE tag carries the handler, so the pattern matches a tag interior rather than the attribute name alone. This was found by the first host harness rejecting a correct implementation, which is the right way round to find it.
nonGoalsNote: A group may carry a `nonGoals` list: payloads the floor deliberately does NOT catch, with the reason. They are recorded and never asserted. Stating a known limit is what makes the rest of the family a gate rather than a wishlist, and a reader who meets silence instead has to re-derive it.
